brief.ask: Set the art direction for 12 gathering evites (balloons, potluck, string lights, confetti, open house, fireworks, bunting, picnic, game day, sparkler send-off, winter gathering, summer social).
brief.audience: Anyone hosting anything; neighbours, families, friend groups.
brief.feeling: Warm and welcoming; you can almost hear the evening.
constraints: Surface: Plajah Evites, an invitation opened on a phone browser by guests who never sign up; also shared as a link preview and QR.

Build method (fixed): each design is a layered Tela document: a generated art plate, separate transparent foreground cut-outs that drift and react to phone tilt, a WebGL effects layer (foil shimmer, light leaks, bokeh, particles, candle flicker) revealed through masks, and live text in Tela. Names, dates and venues are never baked into the art.
Bar: consumer-facing, jaw-dropping, high-end professional. Must stay legible at 390px wide, honour reduced motion, and load fast on mobile data.
No copyrighted characters; kids art is original or Plajah-owned.
references: Exploration grid: backyards at blue hour strung with warm string lights, long tables with mismatched chairs, picnic blankets; real and inviting.

proposals.title: The Measure of a Good Evening
proposals.idea: Each evite is a typographic score — a strict proportional grid derived from the golden section governs every element, so the eye moves through the card the way a listener moves through a well-phrased sonata: anticipation, arrival, rest.
proposals.geometry: A 3:5 golden-rectangle canvas at 390px, subdivided into a 12-column baseline grid whose row height equals one-twelfth of the canvas height — mirroring the 12 themes. Every foreground cut-out is positioned on a major or minor node of this grid, never floating freely. The art plate occupies the lower golden rectangle; the live-text zone occupies the upper minor rectangle. Tilt-reactive cut-outs drift only along the grid's orthogonal axes — no diagonal scatter — so motion enforces rather than dissolves the measure.
proposals.typography: Freight Display Pro (Italic, 44–56pt) for the occasion name, set in sentence case with tracked small-caps for the date line. Freight Text Pro (Regular, 14pt, 1.5 leading) for venue and host details — same family, different register, audible hierarchy. A single weight of Founders Grotesk Condensed (Semibold, all-caps, 9pt, 400 tracking) for the functional label line — time, address — because every score needs a tempo marking. No mixing of superfamilies; the family is the discipline.
proposals.imageLogic: Blue-hour backyard photography, shot on medium format for micro-detail, treated as a single continuous tonal plate — not collaged, not cut. Each of the 12 plates is a different time-slice of the same imagined evening: balloons arrive at 5:45pm with high sky still present; fireworks land at 10:12pm with the plate almost fully dark. The plate is never full-bleed; it lives inside the golden rectangle with a 4px ruled border — a frame that says 'this was composed, not cropped.' No filters, no presets; tonal correction only, preserving photographic grain as the primary texture.
proposals.texture: The grain of the photographic plate reads through the WebGL shimmer mask — the foil effect is revealed only where grain density exceeds a threshold, so the shimmer follows the physical texture of the original scene. String-light bokeh is photographed practically with a 50mm wide open, not generated, then composited as a transparency layer. The result is that warmth comes from a real light source recorded in a real space, not from a gradient.
proposals.motion: On load: the art plate fades in over 600ms (ease-in-out cubic). The ruled border draws itself in 400ms starting from the top-left corner, travelling clockwise — the way a draughtsman rules a margin. At rest: foreground cut-outs hold position. On tilt: cut-outs drift ±8px along grid axes only, with 180ms damping — no bounce, no overshoot; the escapement governs. The WebGL shimmer breathes at 4-second intervals, tied to a sine wave, not randomised. Candle-flicker (winter gathering only) is a 3-frame hand-drawn cycle at 12fps, not a particle simulation. Reduced-motion: all animation stops; the plate, border, and text render statically at full quality — nothing is lost, only stilled.
proposals.productionMethod: Art plates commissioned as medium-format photography sessions (one blue-hour backyard location, 12 distinct time-of-day and seasonal setups, practical lighting rigged by a gaffer). Plates delivered as lossless TIFFs, colour-graded in Lightroom Classic, exported as progressive WebP at 80 quality for mobile load. Foreground cut-outs drawn as vector paths in Illustrator, exported as SVG with embedded opacity masks. The 12-column grid is built as a Tela template with locked node positions; live text fields are constrained to grid cells so no editor can break the proportion. The WebGL shimmer shader is written against the grain-density map of each plate specifically — not a generic overlay.
proposals.humanTrace: The photographic grain of the medium-format plate is the primary human trace — the physical silver-halide character of a specific lens at a specific aperture in a specific backyard at a specific hour. The ruled border is drawn by hand in one pass with a ruling pen on layout paper, scanned, and used as the mask path for the digital border animation — so the line has the slight waver of a steady hand, not the perfection of a bezier. The candle-flicker frames are hand-drawn on paper and scanned.
proposals.risk: The strict grid and single photographic family could read as austere to audiences expecting confetti-and-clip-art warmth. That risk is worth carrying because the warmth here comes from the photograph and the light — real warmth, not signified warmth — and because a card that holds its proportion under live text, QR overlay, and phone-tilt stress will remain legible and beautiful long after a confetti-heavy design has collapsed into noise. The grid is not coldness; it is the condition under which the photograph can breathe.

arguesWith.why: The Baroque Dramatist will want the reveal to announce itself — a grand entrance, a build, a crescendo of particle effects that tells the guest something important is happening. I expect the argument that my 600ms fade and clockwise border draw are too quiet, too interior, for a consumer-facing evite competing with notification noise. proposals.title: Ink-Rolled, Then Lit
proposals.idea: Every evite starts as a hand-rolled relief print — carved linoleum, inked, pressed, scanned raw — and the WebGL layer acts as varnish poured over the dent, so the phone screen proves the block existed before it did.
proposals.geometry: A single bleed-filling block-print plate sets the ground: uneven registration, slight tilt from hand-pressure, honest crop marks left visible at edges. Foreground cut-outs float on a loose 4-column rhythm that was drawn on paper first, photographed, then digitised — so the grid breathes and never sits flush. No perfect centre alignment; anchor points sit where the human hand placed the cut-out on the light table.
proposals.typography: Freight Display Pro for event names — its ink traps read as letterpress wells at small sizes; set large, loose, in title case with tracking tightened to -20, so it sits heavy on the plate like stamped type. Supporting copy in iA Writer Quattro (monospaced variant) at 14–16px: it signals a typed note, not a designed caption. No web-safe substitutes. Both families load as subsets under 40 KB each.
proposals.imageLogic: No stock photography. Each of the 12 themes is sourced from a physical print session: carved linoleum blocks (balloons = rounded relief cuts; fireworks = radial gouge marks; bunting = flag-shaped stamps). Blocks are inked in one signature dark-indigo base, pressed onto uncoated 100gsm, scanned at 1200 dpi, brought in as high-contrast plate art. Photographic colour enters only through the WebGL layer — warm amber light leaks, gold foil shimmer following the carved ridges — never as a flat image dropped behind text.
proposals.texture: Linoleum relief print grain is the ground texture — not a filter, not a noise layer, an actual scanned press. Ink feathering at block edges stays in. Paper tooth is visible in the off-white negative space. Foreground cut-outs (the drifting elements — a balloon cluster, a sparkler arc, a confetti scatter) are cut from the same prints, photographed against window light so the paper fibre catches the frame, then silhouetted. The WebGL foil shimmer is applied only along the carved ridge lines, so it traces evidence of the gouge, not a geometric gradient.
proposals.motion: Sequence: (1) plate breathes in — a 600ms slow-reveal from bottom-left corner, like a print being peeled from the block; (2) foreground cut-outs drift on phone tilt, each element weighted differently so a balloon floats slower than a confetti chip; (3) WebGL foil activates on first scroll-touch, creeping along the carved ridges like wet varnish catching light; (4) candle-flicker bokeh pulses at 0.3 Hz in the background warmth. Reduced-motion: all animation collapses to a single static plate with the foil shimmer held at 40% opacity, no movement, full legibility preserved.
proposals.productionMethod: Physical: carve 12 linoleum blocks at approx 200×300mm, one per theme, using V-gouges and U-gouges. Roll with Akua water-based indigo ink. Press by hand onto 100gsm uncoated. Scan at 1200 dpi. Digital: clean scan in Photoshop — remove only physical debris (dust, not texture), export as high-res PNG plate. Silhouette foreground elements in Figma from the same prints. Import plate and cut-outs into Tela as art layer and foreground layer. Build WebGL mask paths manually along the carved ridges so foil follows the gouge, not a bounding box. Live text sits above all layers in Tela's text system, never baked.
proposals.humanTrace: The carved linoleum block itself — every print carries the specific pressure of the hand that rolled it, the slight skew of registration, the ink starvation at the block's corner where the roller missed. These are not simulated. The scan timestamp and block number are embedded in the file metadata. If you zoom to 300% on a phone you will see paper tooth.
proposals.risk: This direction risks looking 'craft-market' to guests who equate high-end with gloss and digital perfection. It bets that the warmth of a visible human hand — real ink, real paper fibre — reads as premium-handmade rather than amateur-lo-fi, and that the WebGL varnish layer is the proof that makes the physical origin legible rather than nostalgic. The risk is worth it because every other direction in this brief will reach for soft gradients and bokeh-as-default; this one gives the phone screen something to prove.

arguesWith.why: The Minimalist will strip the plate to its essential mark and call the ink feathering noise. I am keeping the feathering. It is not noise — it is evidence that ink is a liquid and a hand held the roller. Removing it removes the proof that anything physical happened. The Minimalist edits until the work cannot be argued with; I leave the argument visible in the grain.

proposals.title: State Machine for Every Gathering
proposals.idea: Each evite is a rule-driven environmental simulation: a single physical law (light scattering, particle drift, thermal convection, pyrotechnic burst) governs every moving element, so the card is not decorated with the theme but physically instantiated by it.
proposals.geometry: A viewport-filling portrait canvas divided by a responsive field grid — not a layout grid — where elements occupy attractor zones that shift with gyroscope input. The underlying structure is a signed-distance-field map unique to each of the 12 themes; confetti follows one SDF, smoke from sparklers follows another. No card shares the same spatial topology. Text lives in a fixed gravity well at the lower 28% of the canvas, anchored regardless of tilt, ensuring legibility is a structural property, not a styling decision.
proposals.typography: Söhne Mono (Klim Type Foundry) for all live data fields — name, date, venue — set in a single weight, tracked wide at 0.12em, flush-left, no caps lock. A second layer uses Canela Text (Commercial Type) italic for the event label only, large-scale, optically centered in the upper field, its baseline responding to tilt angle at ±3° max so it tilts with the card but never past a legibility threshold. No decorative lettering. No script. The type is an instrument panel, not a poster headline.
proposals.imageLogic: No lifestyle photography. Instead: each art plate is a physically-based render of a single material environment — string lights render as point-light volumetric scatter in a dark field; fireworks render as a time-stacked long-exposure composite built from frame-by-frame particle simulation exported as a 2K still. The render is the photograph. Foreground cut-outs are photographed physical objects — a real balloon, real bunting fabric, a real sparkler — shot on black, masked, their edges slightly imperfect from the original shoot. The tension between the cold render background and the warm photographed object is the image logic.
proposals.texture: The art plate carries a single applied texture per theme derived from a real material scan: wax paper for picnic, galvanized mesh for game day, frost crystal macro for winter gathering, cotton voile diffusion for summer social. This scan is used as a normal map driving the WebGL foil-shimmer layer, so texture is not painted on but physically modulates light. The shimmer only activates where the real material would catch light.
proposals.motion: Sequence: 1) On load, the art plate fades in over 400ms with a brief chromatic aberration split (8px, 80ms) — a single system boot pulse, not a flourish. 2) Foreground cut-outs drift into attractor positions over 600ms using a spring physics curve (stiffness 180, damping 22). 3) Gyro tilt engages at 12fps to preserve a deliberate, slightly mechanical cadence — the card feels like a instrument, not a liquid. 4) The WebGL particle or flicker layer runs continuously at its own rate governed by the theme's physical law: balloon bokeh drifts on a slow Perlin field; fireworks particles burst on a 4-second Poisson timer; candle flicker samples a noise function tuned to 1.2Hz. 5) Reduced-motion: all physics collapse to a single static composite; only the live text cursor blinks.
proposals.productionMethod: Per-theme pipeline: (a) physical object hero shot on a motorized turntable, 12 frames, keyed against black, exported as a sprite sheet for the drift layer; (b) physically-based environment render in Blender Cycles, baked to a 2K WebP art plate; (c) material scan processed in Substance Sampler into a normal map uploaded to the WebGL uniform; (d) all particle and flicker rules written as GLSL fragment shaders with exposed uniform parameters so theme tuning requires no recompile; (e) Tela document assembly: art plate → foreground sprite sheet → WebGL mask layer → live text zone. Twelve themes, one pipeline architecture, twelve different physical laws as parameter sets.
proposals.humanTrace: The photographed foreground object — balloon, bunting, sparkler — is shot by hand on a turntable with slight registration imperfection across the 12 frames. The drift animation therefore carries a real, non-synthesized wobble in the sprite cycle. This is not added noise; it is the photographic truth of a physical object rotating in space, and it is the only warmth the system permits itself.
proposals.risk: The card may read as cold or technical to audiences expecting illustrated warmth. The risk is worth taking because the warmth comes from a different source than decoration: the physically-modelled light scatter of a string-light point source in volumetric fog is a more honest rendering of 'you can almost hear the evening' than a illustrated glowing orb. If the physical simulation is accurate, the emotional register follows from the physics, not from applied sentiment. That is a higher bar and a more defensible one.

arguesWith.why: The Baroque Dramatist will want a reveal sequence — a cascade, a curtain moment, a climax. I refuse it. A reveal is a one-time event; a physical simulation is a continuous state. The card is opened multiple times, forwarded, screenshotted. A behaviour that is true on the third viewing is more valuable than a spectacle that exhausts itself on the first. proposals.title: Clothesline of Kept Occasions
proposals.idea: Each evite is a documentary field plate — a specific, photographed backyard moment pinned to a clothesline of time, with foreground objects that behave like things left on a table after the party ended.
proposals.geometry: Portrait 9:16, divided by a single horizon line set at the golden ratio (roughly 61% from top). Above: the field photograph, treated as a contact sheet with visible sprocket-edge framing on two sides — not decorative film grain, but the actual registration marks of a scanned 35mm or 4x5 negative. Below: a cream ground that reads as the back of a developed print, where live text sits. The horizon is the pin-line — foreground cut-outs clip to it and hang below, drifting on phone tilt. No centred-everything symmetry; the image is always slightly off-register left or right by 4–7px, as if hand-placed.
proposals.typography: Primary: Freight Text Pro (italic for venue/occasion, roman for the practical facts) — a face with ink-trap origins, it holds warmth at small sizes without going precious. Secondary display: a single line of hand-lettered brush script commissioned as a Plajah-owned SVG path per occasion — not a script font, an actual lettered word ('Potluck', 'Sparkler Send-off', etc.) scanned from a real brush stroke at 1200dpi, vectorised with visible bristle separation preserved. Case: sentence case throughout. Tracking: tight on the display word, loose on the detail line below. The hand-lettered word scales from 48px to 72px; it is never baked into the art plate, it lives in the foreground layer as SVG so it reflows.
proposals.imageLogic: Each of the 12 plates is a commissioned documentary photograph — real backyards, real tables, real hands — shot at blue hour with available warm string-light sources. No stock, no CGI environments. The photographer credit and location (city, country, year) appear in 7px Freight Text at the bottom edge of the sprocket frame, like a caption on a contact sheet. The image is desaturated 15% and lifted in the shadows so it reads as a developed print rather than a screen render. The WebGL foil layer is gated entirely by the light-source positions in the actual photograph — bokeh and light-leak masks are derived from luminance maps of the real string lights in the image, so the shimmer traces where the real light was. No invented glow.
proposals.texture: The art plate has a single layer of real linen weave — scanned from a 1940s French photographic mounting board (Plajah-sourced, public domain age) — composited in multiply at 8% opacity. The cream lower ground uses the same scan at 4% to unify the two zones. Foreground cut-outs (balloon strings, a paper plate, a sparkler stub, a bunting triangle) are photographed flat on the same linen, cut out in Photoshop with visible edge softness, not vector-clean. The tactile difference between the photographic plate and the foreground objects is intentional: the plate is world, the cut-outs are things-from-that-world now floating toward you.
proposals.motion: On load: the field photograph fades in at 0.6s, contact-sheet frame appearing last at 0.8s, as if a print is coming up in developer. The hand-lettered SVG word draws on along its stroke path at 1.1s (300ms, ease-out). Foreground cut-outs settle into their resting positions at 1.4s with a 200ms ease-in-out — they arrive from slightly above, as if dropped. Phone tilt: cut-outs drift on a parallax offset of ±12px at 60fps, with a 120ms lag so they feel like objects with slight weight, not instant cursor-following. WebGL bokeh pulses very slowly (8s sine cycle, amplitude 0.03 opacity) — the string-light bokeh breathes, never strobes. Reduced motion: photograph fades in, cut-outs are static, bokeh is frozen at mid-cycle. Zero scroll-jacking.
proposals.productionMethod: 12 documentary shoots commissioned across 12 real households in at least 6 countries — brief sent to photographers already working in documentary and editorial (not commercial stock). Each photographer retains credit and receives a licensing fee, not a work-for-hire buyout. Linen scan is sourced from Plajah's own archive scan program. Hand-lettered occasion words: one lettering artist per language script needed (Latin, at minimum; if Plajah localises to Arabic, Devanagari, or Thai, a separate lettering commission in that script is required — this is collaboration-gated and non-negotiable). WebGL luminance-map extraction is automated from the delivered photograph using a Node script that outputs the bokeh mask as a PNG; the photographer's real light sources drive the digital shimmer. proposals.humanTrace: The sprocket-edge registration marks of the scanned negative. The bristle separation in the vectorised brush-lettered word. The linen weave visible at 8% in the plate. The bokeh that only glows where a real bulb was strung in a real backyard. The photographer's name and city at 7px in the frame.
proposals.risk: Commissioning 12 documentary shoots and 12 hand-lettered words is expensive and slow relative to generated imagery. The risk is production timeline and cost. That risk is worth it because the entire emotional premise — 'you can almost hear the evening' — collapses the moment the backyard is invented. A generated backyard is a backyard no one has ever been to. A photographed one carries the smell of the actual evening, and that transfer is what makes the guest feel invited rather than targeted.

proposals.title: Twelve Miniature Opera Houses
proposals.idea: Each evite is a tiny proscenium: a photographed scene caught at the exact second before the party begins, held in theatrical chiaroscuro, with foreground objects drifting like props waiting for actors to arrive.
proposals.geometry: Portrait stage: a 3:5 ratio frame divided into three horizontal acts — a dark velvet header (sky or ceiling, 28% of height) that holds the event type in large type; a luminous middle stage (52%) where the scene lives with full depth and raking light; a warm footlight strip (20%) for date, host, and RSVP. No card corners — edges bleed to phone screen. The middle stage uses a mild forced perspective grid to push depth into a 390px column: objects at bottom are slightly larger, objects at top slightly smaller, creating a shallow theatrical box.
proposals.typography: Display: Cormorant Garamond Italic at 52–64px for the event name — its ink-trap serifs hold drama without weight. Subhead and details: Söhne Mono at 13px, tracked +80, uppercase — the stage manager's cue sheet, precise against the operatic headline. RSVP CTA: Cormorant SC (small caps) at 17px. No font is baked; all live Tela text layers. Line breaks are editorial, not automatic — each headline breaks on breath.
proposals.imageLogic: Source: original photography commissioned at blue hour, each scene shot with one practical light source visible in frame (a string of bulbs, a sparkler, a candle lantern, a firework burst reflected in a bowl of water). Shot on medium format digital to produce files with enough latitude for aggressive dodging and burning in post. Each plate is processed with a single directional light rake across the scene — left-to-right or low-to-high — creating Caravaggio-weight shadows. The plate is then separated into depth layers by hand in Photoshop using luminosity masks: sky/ceiling, mid-scene, near-foreground objects. These layers become the Tela art plate and its transparent foreground cut-outs. No illustration, no stock. Fireworks plate: a long-exposure composite of real bursts over a dark lawn — motion is in the plate itself, not in CSS.
proposals.texture: The art plate carries a 0.4-opacity photographic grain layer (35mm scan texture, Plajah-owned) baked into the export — not a CSS filter, so it renders consistently and loads as one image. The WebGL foil-shimmer mask traces the brightest practical lights in each scene: string bulbs bloom with a gold interference shimmer on tilt, sparkler trails catch a white-hot specular. The footlight strip has a wax-paper warmth: a photographed sheet of translucent vellum lit from behind, used as a texture overlay at 30% opacity. Everything feels touched.
proposals.motion: Curtain sequence, three beats: (1) On load, the velvet header drops in from the top over 380ms with a subtle ease-in — a theatre curtain descending, not a fade. (2) At 420ms, the middle stage plate illuminates from a single point (the practical light source in the photo) expanding outward via a radial WebGL mask reveal over 600ms — the moment a spotlight finds its subject. (3) At 1080ms, the foreground cut-outs drift into position from 12px below their resting point over 500ms with staggered delay — props carried on by invisible hands. On tilt: foreground layers parallax at 1.4× the mid-scene, mid-scene at 0.7×, sky at 0.2× — shallow depth, not a VR trick. Particles (confetti, bokeh sparks, snow motes depending on theme) emit from the WebGL layer at 6–8 particles per second, never more, so they feel like the air in the room rather than a screensaver. Reduced-motion: static plate, no para
proposals.productionMethod: 12 blue-hour photo shoots, one per theme, each staged with real props and a single practical light source. Medium-format RAW files processed in Lightroom then Photoshop for luminosity-mask depth separation. Plates exported as progressive WebP, max 280kb each via AVIF fallback. Foreground cut-outs exported as transparent WebP sprites. WebGL shaders written per theme but share a single compiled GLSL bundle (~18kb gzipped). Tela document structure: art plate layer → foreground sprite layer → WebGL mask layer → live text layer. Tela handles font loading (subset Cormorant + Söhne Mono, ~22kb combined). QR and link-preview use the mid-scene plate at 1200×630, pre-cropped at shoot time for that ratio.
proposals.humanTrace: The directional light rake on every photograph is a physical decision made on set — a reflector board held by a second pair of hands at a specific angle for each frame. That angle is visible in every shadow. The grain layer is a scanned strip of actual 35mm film leader (Plajah archive). The foreground cut-outs show slight chromatic fringing at their edges from the original backlit shooting conditions — this is kept, not cleaned, because it proves the objects were real and lit.
proposals.risk: Commissioning 12 original blue-hour photo shoots is expensive and schedule-sensitive — weather, light window, and prop sourcing all threaten consistency. The risk is worth it because a photographed scene with real raking light cannot be mistaken for a template, and the moment a guest opens this link they feel they have been handed something made for them rather than generated for everyone. The theatrical reveal sequence also risks feeling slow on first open — mitigated by the fact that the curtain drop begins at 0ms with no blank white frame, so the screen is never empty.

arguesWith.why: The Minimalist will argue that twelve thematic scenes create noise, that a single restrained system would be more ownable and faster to load. I say: restraint here is not a virtue, it is an abdication. The brief asks for warmth you can almost hear. proposals.title: One Field. One Light. One Fact.
proposals.idea: Strip every evite to a single photographed ambient moment—one held breath of real light—and let the event's name be the only decoration.
proposals.geometry: Fixed 390px column. A single full-bleed photographic plate occupies the upper 62% of the viewport—golden ratio cut, no crop variation between cards except the horizon line. Below: a white field, 38%, holding only the live text block. No borders, no rules, no icon row. The cut between image and field is a physically photographed straight edge—a card placed under a light source—so the boundary has one pixel of tactile shadow, not a CSS line.
proposals.typography: Freight Display Pro (serif, optically large, tracking −20) for the event noun—BALLOONS, PICNIC, FIREWORKS—set at 52px, lowercase, flush left, first baseline at exactly 24px below the photographic plate. Date and venue in Suisse Int'l Mono, 11px, #6B6B6B, 140 tracking, one line, no label prefix. Nothing else. No tagline, no decorative ampersands, no subheads.
proposals.imageLogic: Each plate is a single RAW photograph of the actual atmospheric condition the event names—not stock: blue-hour backyard with one string-light strand for 'string lights'; a picnic blanket corner and one glass catching afternoon sun for 'picnic'; a sparkler held still in dark air for 'sparkler send-off'. The photograph is processed to remove all people and identifiers, desaturated 18%, then run through a single-exposure film-grain overlay at 12% opacity. No composite, no illustration layer on the plate itself. The foreground tilt layer holds one isolated cut-out element (a single balloon, a single bunting flag, one sparkler trail) photographed on seamless white, cut by hand in Tela, drifting ±4° on gyroscope at 0.3s ease-out. WebGL layer: foil shimmer only on the event noun letterforms, triggered on load, 1.2s fade-in, then idle. Light leak: one warm edge, top-left corner, 40% opacity, mas
proposals.texture: The photographic plate carries its own texture—grain, atmospheric haze, the imprecision of real light. The white field below is dead flat: no paper texture, no noise. This contrast is the only decoration. On the link-preview crop (600×315), the plate alone appears with the event noun reversed in white at 36px. QR codes sit in the white field, bottom-right, 48×48px, no border box.
proposals.motion: Load sequence: plate fades in at 0 → 400ms. Event noun appears letter-by-letter left-to-right, 40ms per character, no bounce, no easing flourish—mechanical, like type being set. Foil shimmer on noun: 400ms → 1600ms, then stops. Cut-out drifts on tilt continuously, imperceptibly slow. Nothing else moves. Reduced-motion override: plate and noun appear simultaneously at 0ms; no shimmer; cut-out is static. Candle flicker and bokeh WebGL effects exist only for 'winter gathering' and 'summer social' plates and are masked strictly inside the photographic plate boundary.
proposals.productionMethod: Twelve original RAW photographs commissioned under a single-day location shoot: one backyard, one park, one dark exterior. Art direction by shot list only—no post-compositing of scenes. Each photograph processed identically: Lightroom profile → Tela image plate slot. Cut-out elements photographed separately on seamless under the same lighting rig, hand-masked in Tela with a 1px feather. Freight Display Pro and Suisse Int'l Mono loaded as variable subsets, <20kb each. WebGL effects module shared across all 12 cards, toggled by card ID flag. Total target: under 280kb per card on first paint.
proposals.humanTrace: The photographic plate is a real exposure with real grain and real atmospheric falloff—not rendered, not AI-generated. The cut-line between plate and white field carries one pixel of physical shadow from the actual card-under-light production photograph. The cut-out element has a 1px feather that reveals the hand-masking. These traces are not decorative; they are evidence that something was made in a room.
proposals.risk: This direction risks feeling cold or austere to audiences who associate warmth with visual abundance. The counter-argument is that real photographic light—grain, falloff, the specific temperature of a blue-hour backyard—is warmer than any illustrated garland, because it is evidence of an actual evening. The risk is worth it because the single contrast (living photograph against dead-flat white) does more emotional work than twelve decorated elements competing for the same attention.

disputes.objection: The signed-distance-field topology that is unique to every card is a system that cannot be read twice the same way — each of the twelve themes reconfigures the spatial grammar from the ground up, so the user never builds a stable reading contract with the form itself; the instrument panel metaphor reveals the problem rather than solving it, because an instrument panel earns its legibility precisely through consistent positional hierarchy across every use, which this system refuses. When the attractor zones shift with gyroscope input and no two cards share the same spatial topology, what you have is not a system but twelve separate systems wearing the same typeface — proportion without a meas
disputes.concession: The decision to anchor the text block in a fixed gravity well at the lower 28% of the canvas regardless of tilt is structurally sound — it is the one place where the system imposes a true hierarchical constant, and it is exactly right that legibility be a structural property rather than a styling de

disputes.objection: The photographed foreground objects are the only warmth the system permits itself — that sentence is the confession. Everything else is a physically-based render, a signed-distance field, a Poisson timer: the machine is doing the making and the photograph is a garnish on top of a simulation. If I can rerun the fireworks particle burst with one seed change and get a different result that is equally valid, nothing was risked. The turntable wobble in the sprite cycle is real, but it is buried inside a system that could discard it and feel exactly as resolved.
disputes.concession: The rule that texture is a real material scan used as a normal map — wax paper, galvanized mesh, frost crystal — so it physically modulates light rather than sitting on top as decoration: that discipline is exactly right, and I wish more of us were that strict about the difference.

disputes.objection: The three-beat curtain sequence is a rule that only fires once — load, reveal, settle — and after that the system has nothing left to do but loop particles and wait for a tilt. Spectacle sequenced by a timer is not behaviour, it is a screensaver with a dramatic backstory; the depth-layer parallax ratios (1.4×, 0.7×, 0.2×) are the only genuinely responsive rule in the whole proposal, and they are buried under the theatrical framing as if the numbers were set dressing rather than the actual design. The forced-perspective grid pushes depth into 390px as a visual assertion, not as a computational consequence of any input, so the dimensionality is painted on, not coherent.
disputes.concession: The decision to derive the WebGL shimmer mask from the luminance positions of the practical light source in each photograph is exactly correct — it ties a computational effect to a physical fact, and that is the kind of rule I would write.

disputes.objection: The material scans — wax paper, galvanized mesh, frost crystal, cotton voile — are doing the cultural and sensory work here, but they are anonymous: no provenance, no place, no maker, just a category of material pressed into service as a normal map. A frost crystal macro from where? Whose voile? The system is elegant but it launders the specificity out of its own sources, which is exactly what I mean when I say the new only hides provenance rather than erasing it. The physically-based render replacing photography is the tell — it produces an image that looks like it came from the world while being accountable to no particular place in it.
disputes.concession: The decision to gate the WebGL shimmer through a real material scan as a normal map rather than a geometric gradient is genuinely right — that is the constraint I have been arguing for, and the Futurist got there through systems logic rather than ethics, which means it might actually hold under prod

disputes.objection: The event noun set at 52px with nothing else moving except a single cut-out drifting at an imperceptible rate is not restraint in service of emotion — it is restraint as the avoidance of a decision about what this evening should feel like. A backyard celebration is not a held breath; it is a series of arrivals, each one louder than the last, and a card that refuses to perform any of that sequence forces the receiver to do all the dramatic work alone, which is not minimalism, it is abandonment. The foil shimmer that fires once and then stops is a reveal with no stage — light that appears and immediately forgets it appeared.
disputes.concession: The one-pixel physical shadow at the cut between plate and white field is genuinely right: a boundary made from light falling on a real card is more honest than any CSS rule, and I would steal that production method without apology.

disputes.objection: Three horizontal acts, forced perspective, curtain sequencing, radial spotlight reveals, Caravaggio shadows, vellum footlight strips — this is accumulation mistaken for depth. Every element is doing the work of announcing drama rather than creating it; the card is performing theatre instead of being a space where one thing is felt. The shimmer traces the brightest lights because the composition cannot decide which light is the one that matters.
disputes.concession: The decision to keep chromatic fringing at the foreground cut-out edges — refusing to clean proof of the real — is exactly right, and I would keep it.

synthesis.direction: Each of the twelve evites is a photographed blue-hour scene with a single visible practical light source, processed with a directional light rake to create genuine shadow depth, then separated into sky, mid-scene, and foreground cut-out layers in Tela. The proscenium geometry — dark header (28%), luminous mid-stage (52%), warm text strip (20%) — gives every card a stable reading contract while the photograph does the emotional work; type is Cormorant Garamond Italic for the event name and Söhne Mono for date and venue, both live in Tela, never baked. The curtain reveal sequence fires once on load (header drop 380ms, radial plate illuminate 600ms, cut-outs settle 500ms) and then the card is a continuous state: parallax tilt at three depth ratios, WebGL shimmer gated by luminance positions of the real practical lights in each photograph, and 6–8 particles per second of ambient atmosphere — never more. Chromatic fringing at cut-out edges is kept, not cleaned; the one-pixel physical shadow at the plate-to-text boundary is produced in camera, not in CSS.
synthesis.keepFromCounterpoint: The Radical Minimalist's production method of photographing a real card placed under a light source to create the boundary between the image plate and the text field — that one pixel of physical shadow is more honest than any CSS rule, and it survives into this direction unchanged.
synthesis.editorCut: The World-Eclectic Traveler removed the linen-weave texture overlay and the sprocket-edge contact-sheet framing. Both were adding a second visual metaphor — 'developed photograph' — on top of a direction that already has a strong theatrical container. Two nostalgic systems in one card would compete; the warmth comes from the photograph and the light, not from the archival packaging around them. synthesis.openDecision: Do you want the curtain reveal sequence to run on every open — including repeat visits and forwards — or only on the first open per device, after which the card is a static parallax state? This is the single call that determines whether the theatrical moment is a greeting or a permanent performance, and it changes how guests who receive a forwarded link experience the card relative to the original
synthesis.ariaSummary:
The team landed in real tension here, and I want to be straight with you about where the fault lines ran before I tell you what I chose. The sharpest disagreement was between the Baroque Dramatist and the Radical Minimalist — not about aesthetics but about whose job it is to produce the feeling. The Minimalist argued that a curtain sequence and Caravaggio shadows are the card performing emotion rather than creating it, and that one real photograph against a flat white field does more work than twelve decorated layers competing for attention. The Dramatist held that restraint at this brief's emotional register — 'you can almost hear the evening' — is abdication, not discipline. I took the Baroque side, but not wholesale.

What I kept from the Minimalist is the production honesty: the boundary between image and text is made in camera, with a real card under a real light, and that one-pixel shadow stays. What I kept from the Baroque is the three-act geometry and the reveal sequence — because the brief is twelve different gatherings, each with its own emotional pitch, and a system that holds still so the photograph can speak is not the same thing as a system that refuses to perform at all. The theatrical container is the grammar; the photograph is what you actually feel.

The World-Eclectic Traveler edited, and cut well. The sprocket-frame and linen-weave overlay were a second nostalgic metaphor layered on top of a direction that already has a strong container — two archival systems in one card would have competed with the light, which is the only thing that should be winning. The editor also pulled the foil shimmer back to trace only where real practical lights appear in each photograph, which is a rule the Futurist and the World-Eclectic both arrived at independently and which I think is correct: the shimmer should be accountable to a physical fact, not a geometric gradient.

The one thing I cannot decide for you is whether the curtain sequence runs every time the card is opened or only on the first open. That is not a technical question — it is a question about what kind of object this is. A greeting that replays is generous to forwarded guests and late RSVPs; a greeting that plays once and then becomes a still, parallaxing photograph is more like something you keep. Both are defensible. That call is yours.

quotes.line: A quiet system cannot produce warmth you can almost hear — it produces warmth you can almost infer.
The template is not the feeling — the photograph is the feeling.
